output: Two small studies looked at using medicines called glucocorticosteroids to treat a condition called primary sclerosing cholangitis. In one study, a medicine called hydrocortisone caused more side effects like pancreatitis and cholangitis, and didn't help with the condition better than a normal salt solution. In another study, a different medicine called prednisone raised the levels of a chemical called bilirubin more than another medicine called budesonide. Neither study found clear benefits for treating the condition. The first study had to stop because it caused too many side effects. Overall, there's not enough good evidence to show whether these medicines work or not for this condition. Using medicines through the bile duct might cause serious problems. More research is needed.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 5193 participants. It found that taking zinc helped reduce the chance of getting pneumonia by about 13%, which means it's a bit less likely to get sick with pneumonia. It also reduced the number of times people already had pneumonia by about 41%. When doctors check for pneumonia using tests like chest X-rays, zinc helps even more, reducing the chance of getting pneumonia by about 21%. But when doctors use a looser definition of pneumonia based on how a person looks, zinc didn't seem to help. Taking zinc seems to be good at preventing pneumonia, especially when doctors use more specific tests to look for it.

output: This review looked at six studies with 157 people who had diabetic foot ulcers. The studies compared foam dressings to other types of dressings like basic ones, alginate dressings, and hydrocolloid dressings. So, right now, there's not enough good evidence to say foam dressings work better than other types for healing foot ulcers in people with diabetes. Doctors might want to think about other factors too, like how much the dressings cost and what each type does to manage the fluid in the wounds.

The review looked at 14 studies comparing different types of medicines called TCAs and SSRIs to a placebo (a pretend medicine) for treating depression in primary care. About 1364 people took the real medicines and 919 took the placebo. Most studies lasted about 6 to 8 weeks. When comparing the medicines to the placebo, TCAs seemed to work better, helping more people feel better (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.11-1.38). SSRIs also seemed to help more people (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.43). 

For TCAs, about 9 out of every 10 people who take the medicine will feel better compared to those taking the placebo. For SSRIs, it's about 7 out of every 10. But both medicines can cause side effects, and about 4 out of every 10 people taking TCAs might stop because of side effects, while about 20 out of every 100 people taking SSRIs might do the same. So, while TCAs and SSRIs are good at helping people feel better, they can also cause some problems.

output: The review looked at 30 scoring systems used to measure something called histopathology, which is a way doctors look at tissue samples under a microscope to see if there are signs of healing in people with ulcerative colitis (UC). Out of these 30 systems, only 11 have been checked to see if they work well when used by the same person (intra-rater reliability) and by different people (inter-rater reliability). Some systems have been checked for whether they cover everything they should (content validation), how well they match what we think they should match (criterion validity), and how sensitive they are to changes (responsiveness). The Nancy Index and Robarts Histopathology Index have been checked for the most things, like if they work well and if they match what we expect. But none of the systems have been fully checked to make sure they are the best. To find the best system, we need more research to fully check how well each system works.

output: In five studies with 694 infants, using a longer inflation time (IT) was linked to more air leaks, which means the lungs didn't seal properly after breathing. This happened more often than expected by chance. But it didn't seem to cause more babies to have a condition called bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Longer ITs might also lead to more babies dying before leaving the hospital. However, these studies were done before new treatments like antenatal steroids and surfactant were widely used. Most of the babies studied had a lung problem called hyaline membrane disease (HMD). The results may not apply to all types of newborns who need extra help breathing. Still, if a baby's lungs aren't working well, doctors should use shorter ITs to help keep their lungs from leaking air.

output: This review looked at ten studies with 33,179 participants to see if vitamin A helps prevent colds and other lung infections in children. Some studies found that giving vitamin A didn't help prevent these infections. Other studies found that it might make some children more likely to get these infections. Three studies said vitamin A didn't affect the number of infections. Two studies found that vitamin A helped prevent infections in children who were already not very healthy, but it didn't help healthy children. Because of this, we shouldn't give vitamin A to all children to prevent these infections. While vitamin A is good at preventing another illness called diarrhea, it doesn't seem to work well for preventing these lung infections. It seems to work best in children who are already not very healthy. Using lower doses of vitamin A might still be helpful and cause fewer side effects.

output: The review found three studies that looked at how a medicine called beclomethasone affects children with mild to moderate asthma. This medicine is usually given twice a day through a special inhaler. The studies lasted from 7 to 12 months. All three found that children who took beclomethasone grew shorter than those who didn't take it. On average, they grew 1.54 cm less per year. If your child needs to use beclomethasone to control their asthma, it's important to use the smallest amount that works well and to watch their growth closely.

output: The review found one study with 156 children who had bronchiolitis, a common lung infection in babies and young children. The children were split into three groups: one group got nebulised salbutamol, another got nebulised saline, and the third got mist in a tent. The study showed that the nebulised salbutamol helped reduce breathing problems (respiratory distress) in the children. The mist in the tent did not help reduce these breathing problems. Steam inhalation is often used to treat bronchiolitis, especially in places where resources are limited. While this study suggests that nebulised salbutamol might be helpful, the mist in the tent did not show any benefit. Because only one study was done, we can't say for sure if mist therapy is ineffective. Right now, there isn't enough information to tell doctors whether to use steam inhalation or mist therapy to help children with bronchiolitis. More studies are needed.

output: This review looked at 11 studies comparing early feeding to delayed feeding in patients who needed special nutrition. Seven studies had information on whether patients died. One study compared feeding through the stomach to feeding through another part of the intestine and couldn't tell if there was a difference. Overall, early feeding might be a bit better for survival and disability, but we need more studies to be sure. These studies should look at both how well patients do and whether they live longer.

output: The review looked at 36 studies involving 6914 people. Different antibiotics were used in the studies, and some people got other illnesses or died in the groups that didn't get antibiotics. Studies that compared getting both topically (on the skin) and systemically (through the body) showed fewer respiratory tract infections (RTIs) and lower death rates in the group that got antibiotics. But studies that just used topically or topically plus systemically didn't find fewer RTIs, though they still didn't see higher death rates. Combining topically and systemically seems to help prevent RTIs and reduce overall deaths in people in intensive care. Using just topically doesn't seem to prevent RTIs, but it also doesn't seem to cause more resistance to antibiotics. More research is needed to fully understand the effects.

output: This review looked at 10 studies where surgeons used either sharp or blunt needles during different surgeries like abdominal closure, caesarean sections, vaginal repairs, and hip replacements. On average, surgeons using sharp needles had one glove tear every three operations, while those using blunt needles had fewer tears. Blunt needles reduced the risk of glove tears by about half compared to sharp needles (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.54). This means they prevent one tear in every six operations. Blunt needles also lowered the number of needle stick injuries reported by surgeons and their assistants. While it took more effort to use blunt needles, it wasn't too hard for most surgeons. The evidence is very strong and reliable. Future research is unlikely to change these findings. Using blunt needles helps protect surgeons and their helpers from getting blood and body fluids on their hands during surgery.

output: This review looked at three studies involving 1166 women with breast cancer who were treated with different ways of combining radiation therapy (RT) and chemotherapy (CT). The studies did not find that one way of giving these treatments was better than another for preventing the cancer from coming back or spreading. However, women who got both treatments together (concurrent chemoradiation) often had more problems like feeling very tired (anaemia), getting red spots on their skin (telangiectasia), and changes in skin colour (pigmentation). Women themselves didn't notice that their appearance changed more with the combined treatments, but doctors did. Also, women didn't have worse side effects like looking less attractive (cosmesis) with the combined treatments. One study found that starting radiation therapy first might make it harder to avoid infections (neutropenic sepsis) compared to starting CT first, but other side effects were similar. Overall, the evidence from these well-done studies suggests that the order of giving CT and RT doesn't seem to make a big difference for preventing the cancer from coming back or spreading, as long as the radiation starts within about 7 months after surgery.

After 3 to 5 months, people who ate sweet potatoes had slightly lower blood sugar levels compared to those who didn't eat them. But the studies weren't perfect and it's hard to know if the sweet potatoes really made the difference. The studies didn't look at serious problems like heart disease or death. Also, they didn't check if eating sweet potatoes made people feel better or do better in their daily lives. There isn't enough good evidence yet to say if sweet potatoes should be used to treat diabetes. To make sure the results are reliable, more studies are needed. These studies should use the same types of sweet potatoes and follow strict rules to make sure everything is done correctly.

output: Two studies looked at different treatments for urethral stricture disease in men. One study compared two surgeries: dilating the urethra and burning it open. It found no difference in how well these treatments worked after three years. Another study compared burning the urethra open right away versus doing a more complex surgery called urethroplasty. In the first six months, men who had the simpler burn surgery needed more follow-up surgeries. After two years, about half of those who had the burn surgery needed more treatment, compared to about a quarter of those who had the more complex surgery. Because there weren't enough men in the studies, we can't say which treatment works better. We also don't know if one treatment is less expensive or causes fewer side effects. To make sure we have good information, we need more studies done by many doctors in different places.

output: This review looked at six studies with 478 babies to see if giving babies a sweet taste before a needle stick (venepuncture) or a pinprick (heel lance) made the babies less painful. Babies who got the sweet taste before the needle stick had less pain than those who got the pinprick. The studies showed that using a sweet taste helps make the needle stick less painful. If a baby needs another needle stick after the first one, it happens less often when a sweet taste is given. Skilled nurses do the needle sticks, and they work better when a sweet taste is used. However, the pinprick is still a bit more painful than the needle stick even with the sweet taste. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at five studies involving 1127 patients to see if removing a stent early after surgery helps prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs) or makes more kidney transplants unsuccessful (MUC). The studies weren't perfect, but they generally followed the right methods. Early removal of the stent didn't seem to lower the chance of MUC. However, it might help prevent UTIs, especially when a special type of stent called a BI stent is used. But when a different type of stent called an externalized PU stent is used, it doesn't seem to help with UTIs. The studies couldn't tell us much about how well this works financially or how it affects quality of life. So, while early removal of the stent might help with UTIs, we're not sure if it increases the risk of making kidney transplants unsuccessful. Using a BI stent seems to be the best way to get the UTI benefit.

output: This review looked at eight studies with about 10,000 people. The studies tested different medicines called statins, along with other medicines like clofibrate and conjugated oestrogen. Statins didn't seem to help prevent strokes overall, but they might slightly lower the chance of another stroke or blood vessel problem in people who have had a stroke or mini-stroke before. Statins did seem to lower the risk of major heart problems, like heart attacks, in people who have had a stroke or mini-stroke. But they didn't seem to help prevent strokes in people who have had bleeding in their brain. It's not clear if starting statins right after a stroke would help. Doctors think that people who have had a stroke or mini-stroke, especially if they already have heart disease, should take statins. More research is needed to know if statins are helpful for everyone who has had a stroke or mini-stroke.

output: The review looked at 32 studies about how editors help make medical papers easier to read and how well they check the references. Only three studies were done properly using a random method. Some changes made by editors, like checking papers carefully, seem to make papers clearer and better written. But it's hard to know if these changes really work because many studies didn't do a good job. Editors often use a set of steps to improve papers, and this seems to reduce mistakes in the parts of papers called abstracts and references. However, giving clear instructions to authors doesn't always help fix problems with references. Making papers follow a specific structure can make them better, but it also makes them longer. Most papers still have mistakes in the references. Overall, there's some evidence that the ways editors work together can make papers better, but more studies are needed to confirm this.

output: This review looked at 23 studies with 724 people to see which treatments work best for a skin condition called PPP. Systemic retinoids and oral PUVA were found to be helpful, especially when used together. Topical steroid under hydrocolloid occlusion also works well. Low dose ciclosporin, tetracycline antibiotics, and Grenz Ray Therapy might help too. But colchicine has lots of side effects and its effectiveness isn't clear. Hydroxycarbamide doesn't seem to work. Some treatments just make the number of pustules go down a little bit, but it's hard to know if they really help much. The review found that there's no single best treatment and that studies need to be done better so people can choose the best option for their condition.

output: Nine high-quality studies with 260 participants looked at different types of exercise therapy for people with multiple sclerosis who are not having a flare-up. The best way to combine the results showed that exercise therapy helps improve muscle strength, how far you can walk, and your ability to do daily activities. It also seems to help with feeling better emotionally. But it didn't seem to help with feeling tired or how you feel about your disability. Exercise therapy didn't work better than other types of exercise for these things. None of the studies showed that exercise therapy caused any harm. This suggests that exercise therapy might be helpful for people with multiple sclerosis who aren't having a flare-up. However, more research is needed to agree on what tests to use and how much exercise is best. Studies should also make sure that the type of exercise and the kind of multiple sclerosis are the same in all parts of the study.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with a total of 2246 people who have atrial fibrillation (AF), a type of irregular heartbeat. The studies tested different ways to help people with AF take their medicine better. Self-tracking plus education didn't seem to help people stick to their medicine schedule much better than usual care. But education did seem to help reduce feelings of worry and sadness in people with AF. Decision-making tools didn't seem to help people make decisions about their medicine better than usual care. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if these types of interventions work well for helping people with AF take their medicine regularly. More studies are needed to find out if these methods work and why some might help while others don't. It's also important to consider how these changes might affect people's mental health over time.

It also helped keep people out of the hospital less often (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0) and made sure they took their medicine better (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.7). Family support didn't seem to make people want to leave treatment more. It also helped families feel better overall. While family support seems helpful, the studies weren't always done well. Better-designed studies would give us more confidence in these results. So, family support might be useful for people with schizophrenia, but we need more good-quality research to be sure.

output: The review looked at four studies with 1154 people aged 50 to 90 who had Alzheimer's disease. Most people in the studies were already taking a medicine called a cholinesterase inhibitor. The studies measured how well people did on tests of memory and thinking skills, and if they had side effects from taking a type of medicine called a statin. When all the studies were put together, the results showed that statins did not help people do better on these tests or have fewer side effects. The studies were done fairly, so we can trust the results. However, the studies did not look at another type of brain problem called vascular dementia (VaD), so we don't know if statins might help with that. Overall, the evidence suggests that statins do not improve memory and thinking skills in people with Alzheimer's disease.

output: Two ways to close the skin after a cesarean section are using non-absorbable staples or absorbable stitches. When comparing these two methods, non-absorbable staples do not cause more infections around the wound compared to stitches. However, staples can sometimes lead to the skin separating from the wound, which might require closing again. This happens more often with staples than with stitches, but it's not always clear if it's a big problem because the staples are often taken out before four days after the surgery. The evidence isn't strong enough to say which method is better overall. Staples and stitches both work similarly in terms of pain, how the scar looks, and how well the wound heals. If staples are removed after three days, there's a higher chance of the skin separating and needing to be closed again. More research is needed to decide which method is best.

output: This review looked at 11 studies involving 38,742 people. Eight studies compared Blood Pressure Lowering Drugs (BPLDs) to a placebo or no treatment, and three compared different blood pressure goals. The studies had different levels of trustworthiness. Overall, BPLDs seemed to reduce the risk of having another stroke (reduced by about 19%) compared to a placebo or no treatment. They also seemed to lower the risk of major health problems like heart attacks or strokes (by about 10%) and might help prevent dementia (by about 12%). When looking at people who were already taking ACE inhibitors or diuretics, BPLDs seemed to reduce the risk of stroke even more. However, the studies comparing different blood pressure goals didn't show clear benefits. The evidence is mostly from studies that used ACE inhibitors or diuretics. We don't have enough information to decide the best blood pressure goal after having a stroke or mini-stroke. More research is needed.

output: This review looked at 56 studies with a total of 4068 participants, mostly people with breast cancer. It found that exercise was better than not exercising at helping reduce fatigue, especially after cancer treatment. The studies showed that aerobic exercises, like running or swimming, worked well to lower fatigue. But other types of exercise, like lifting weights, didn't seem to help as much. The review suggests that aerobic exercise might be helpful for people with cancer who are going through or just finished treatment, especially if they have solid tumors like those in the breast or prostate. More research is needed to find the best kind, length, and time of exercise to help with fatigue.

output: Two studies looked at RhD negative women who received anti-D prophylaxis during pregnancy. Each study gave the women a 1500 IU dose of Rhophylac at week 28 of their pregnancy. Neither study saw any women develop RhD alloimmunization, which is a rare outcome. In one study, the levels of anti-D IgG in the blood were higher after IV administration than after IM administration for about a week. But by two to three weeks later, the levels were about the same for both routes. Both IM and IV injections work well to prevent RhD alloimmunization. output: This review looked at 10 studies with a total of 1896 patients to see if a new type of hospital unit called a NLU helps people recover from serious illnesses. While the studies didn't show a clear benefit in terms of death, they did find that patients who stayed in the NLU were less likely to need to go back to the hospital right away (early readmissions were reduced by about half). Patients also seemed to do better in terms of their daily activities after leaving the hospital. However, the studies also showed that patients spent a bit longer in the hospital. The costs of care were higher in some studies and lower in others. Some studies suggested that patients might be better prepared for going home, but it's not clear if this is just because they stayed longer in the hospital. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if the NLU helps, but it seems to help with some things like getting ready to leave the hospital. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: The review looked at 14 studies with 709 people to see if non-removable casts helped heal foot sores better than other treatments. So, non-removable casts are better at healing foot sores caused by diabetes than removable casts or just dressings. When these casts are used along with stretching the back of the leg, they work even better.

output: This review looked at studies that tested different medicines to help people lose weight. It found 22 studies with a total of 296 people who took fluoxetine, 2036 who took orlistat, and 1047 who took sibutramine. These medicines helped people lose a little bit of weight—about 5.1 kg (95% CI 3.3 - 6.9 kg) with fluoxetine, 2.0 kg (CI 1.3 - 2.8 kg) with orlistat, and 5.1 kg (CI 3.2 - 7.0 kg) with sibutramine. The medicines also helped lower blood sugar levels. But taking these medicines sometimes caused side effects like stomach problems with orlistat, shaking hands with fluoxetine, and fast heartbeat with sibutramine. Other medicines like mazindol, phenmetrazine, and phentermine also helped people lose weight, but not as much as the ones mentioned. There wasn't enough information about some other medicines. Fluoxetine, orlistat, and sibutramine can help people lose a little bit of weight, but the amount is small and we don't know if it's good for you in the long run. The medicine sibutramine might not be safe. There isn't much information about other medicines that can help with weight loss or controlling blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes.

output: This review looked at studies comparing ibuprofen to a sugar pill or other medicines for treating migraine headaches. It found that ibuprofen works better than a sugar pill in reducing headache pain and making you feel better after two hours. The higher dose of ibuprofen (400 mg) was better at relieving headache pain within two hours compared to a lower dose (200 mg). Soluble forms of ibuprofen (which dissolve quickly in the mouth) worked better than regular tablets for quick relief. However, ibuprofen didn't work any better than another medicine called rofecoxib for longer-lasting relief. Most people who took ibuprofen had only mild side effects, like feeling sick or dizzy, which went away quickly. Overall, ibuprofen helps about half of people with migraines feel better, but it doesn't completely stop the pain or other symptoms for most people. More studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: Nine studies looked at feeding preterm babies who are learning to eat normally after being fed through a tube. These studies were not perfect and had some problems like not being able to hide who was getting which food. When comparing responsive feeding (where the baby decides when to eat) to scheduled feeding (where the baby eats at set times), the studies suggested that responsive feeding might help babies start eating solids faster and gain weight more slowly. However, the evidence isn't very strong because the studies weren't well done. It's not clear if this helps babies stay in the hospital longer. The studies didn't ask parents or caregivers about their experiences. So, we don't have strong proof that responsive feeding changes important things for preterm babies or their families. Some studies show that babies who feed when they're hungry might start eating solid foods sooner. But we need more research to know if this is true and if it affects other important things.

Also, ways to make the medicine less likely to cause side effects in mothers need to be studied further.

output: The review looked at six trials with 1758 participants who had mild to moderate heartburn. Most participants were younger adults, but one group was older adults. The trials compared taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) as needed (on-demand) versus every day (continuous). Taking PPIs as needed might make it harder to keep your heartburn away (less 'symptom control'), but it can also reduce how many pills you take each week (less 'drug burden'). People might also feel less satisfied with taking PPIs as needed. The trials didn't look at costs or if stopping the medicine caused any good changes. For people with mild heartburn, using PPIs as needed might cause more stomach upset (like feeling full or getting acid in your throat) but might help you take fewer pills. But we don't know if stopping the medicine has long-term benefits or harms because the studies weren't designed to find out.

output: This review looked at 23 studies that tested different ways to teach young women about sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and safer sex practices. Most of these studies happened in the United States and were done in health clinics. The studies varied in how long they lasted, how much time people spent learning, who gave the information, and what they focused on teaching. Some covered HIV, chlamydia, and other STIs, but not HPV or cervical cancer. Many of the studies found that teaching young women about STIs helped them use condoms more often. But it didn't always work to get them to stop having sex or have less sex. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure how well they worked. It's important to continue studying these methods, especially focusing on HPV and how it can lead to cervical cancer. Future studies should try to answer more questions and see if these methods really help in the long run. They should also look at costs and whether these programs are worth doing. It would be helpful to do more studies in other countries too.

Overall, CRT seems to be the best choice for early-stage disease, but CT might be better for advanced stages. More recent and detailed studies would help us understand these results better.

More research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the risks.

More studies are needed to figure out the best way to use these DNA changes in treatment.

output: This review looked at six studies involving 355 infants to see if continuous distending pressure (CDP) helped them breathe better. The studies were done a long time ago, so it's hard to know if the results apply to modern practices. More research is needed to figure out the best way to use CDP for preterm babies who have trouble breathing.

output: This review looked at 22 studies that tested different hormonal methods to prevent pregnancy, using them in the vagina. output: This review looked at 34 studies with 2169 people who had blepharitis, a condition that causes itchy, red eyes. Some studies used different treatments like antibiotics and lid hygiene, which helps clean the eyelids. Antibiotics helped ease symptoms and get rid of bacteria for people with front blepharitis. Lid hygiene also helped people with both front and back blepharitis. But other treatments like topical steroids and oral antibiotics weren't proven to work better. They should also follow people for at least a year to see if the treatments work long-term.

output: This review looked at different types of metal devices used to fix broken hips in older people. Wound infections, death, and other health problems didn't differ much between the two types of screws. For IMHS and SHS, there weren't big differences in problems like wound infections or death. Intramedullary nails might be better for some broken bones, but more research is needed to know for sure.

output: Three small studies looked at different types of physical therapy after a treatment called BoNT for people who have had a stroke and still have problems moving their arms. The studies were not very good because they had some flaws. The studies found that a special kind of therapy called modified constraint-induced movement therapy (mCIMT) helped people move their arms better and less stiff for up to six months. Also, using a special splint for the elbow and doing regular therapy helped keep the elbow joints from getting too tight. But another type of therapy called task practice therapy with a special electric stimulation didn't help more than just doing the usual therapy. None of the studies looked at children or people with leg problems. Overall, the evidence is not strong enough to say which types of therapy work best for helping arm movement after a stroke. We need more research to figure out the best kinds of therapy and how much is needed to help people move their arms better and feel better.

output: Six studies with 142 children with hemophilia showed that getting medicine regularly (prophylaxis) helps prevent bleeding episodes better than only using it when bleeding starts (on-demand treatment). Specifically, prophylaxis reduced bleeding into joints by about half compared to not using it at all. However, the studies couldn't agree on whether taking the medicine every day or waiting a week between doses works better. Studies in children with hemophilia A found that regular use of the medicine led to fewer joint bleeds. But studies comparing different dosing schedules didn't find one worked better than another. For hemophilia B, weekly injections were linked to fewer joint bleeds than bi-weekly ones. Using the medicine regularly also seemed to cause more problems like infections and blood clots. Strong evidence suggests that regular use helps keep joints healthy in children with hemophilia. But we need more studies to know if this is true for adults and if certain types of medicine work best.

output: This review looked at seven studies comparing high and low levels of a breathing machine setting called PEEP in patients who have trouble breathing. The studies also showed that patients with a condition called ARDS might do better if they use higher levels of PEEP, but this needs more research. Overall, the studies had some differences that make it hard to draw clear conclusions.

output: In this review, 55 studies with 16,154 people who have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) were looked at. Most studies found that using inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for more than six months didn't help keep their lung function from getting worse. However, one big study showed it might help a little bit. Using ICS didn't seem to affect how long people lived. Studies that could pool their results showed that people using ICS had fewer flare-ups of COPD. ICS also seemed to improve how well people felt overall. But, ICS didn't work better for everyone. It didn't depend on whether people got better with oral steroids, if their lungs opened up easily with a puff of air, or if their airways were extra sensitive. Using ICS did make some people more likely to get a fungal infection in their mouth and hoarse voices. Also, people taking ICS had a higher chance of getting pneumonia. Overall, the studies didn't show a clear benefit for bones. The review suggests that people with COPD should talk to their doctors about whether using ICS might help them feel better and have fewer flare-ups, even though there might be some risks involved.

The study found that babies in both groups were breastfed for about four months, but there wasn't much difference between the groups. Rooming-in didn't seem to make babies breastfeed longer. Overall, the study doesn't strongly support or rule out the idea that letting babies stay with their moms more often helps with breastfeeding. More studies are needed to better understand this.

Salbutamol, a medicine used to treat asthma, was found to lower potassium levels faster when given through a nebulizer (inhaled) or a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) compared to a placebo. Nebulized salbutamol worked quickly, with the biggest drop seen about an hour after taking it. Salbutamol also worked as well as insulin and dextrose, but better than bicarbonate. Other medicines like insulin and dextrose were more effective than bicarbonate and aminophylline. None of the studies looked at how well these medicines prevent serious problems. Salbutamol seems to be the best medicine to lower potassium levels quickly, but more research is needed to know if it works better than other options.

output: This review looked at 38 studies with 1828 people to see if a certain type of sugar called non-absorbable disaccharides helps prevent a condition called hepatic encephalopathy, which can happen in people with liver problems. Overall, the sugar might help prevent or treat hepatic encephalopathy, but more research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 13 studies with 16,112 participants. Most studies involved people who had heart problems before. The studies found that taking a type of medicine called fibrates might help prevent some heart problems like strokes and heart attacks. When all the studies were put together, fibrates seemed to lower the chance of having a heart attack by about 16%. They didn't seem to affect how long people lived or the chance of having a stroke. Some studies showed that fibrates might help, but others didn't. This is because one type of fibrates called clofibrate was taken off the market because it had too many side effects. Without clofibrate, fibrates still seemed to help prevent heart attacks, but not strokes. The studies didn't find that fibrates caused more bad side effects. The benefits of fibrates were seen in people of different ages, genders, and those with diabetes. More studies are needed to see if fibrates work well in people who have had a stroke before and are already taking another medicine called statins.

output: This review looked at 17 studies with 1006 participants to see if psychological treatments helped reduce chest pain. The studies found that psychological treatments, especially those using a cognitive-behavioral approach, helped reduce chest pain in the short term. Hypnotherapy might also work. More research is needed to confirm these findings, especially studies that follow people for at least a year.

Most of these studies had problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies also had different ways of deciding what counts as sepsis, which makes it hard to compare them. When we tried to figure out how well IL-6 works, we couldn't get clear answers because the studies were too different. Based on the information we have, IL-6 might help doctors identify sepsis, but it also means that some people who don't have sepsis might think they do, and some who do have sepsis might miss it. This is important because diagnosing sepsis quickly is crucial for treating it properly. More studies are needed to better understand how well IL-6 works and to improve the way doctors use it to diagnose sepsis.

This review looked at 80 studies that compared different types of medicines called NSAIDs (including both regular and special kinds) with a sugar pill (placebo) or another medicine called paracetamol for treating menstrual pain. For women with primary menstrual pain, NSAIDs worked better than the placebo at reducing pain. About 45 to 53 out of every 100 women who took NSAIDs felt much better, compared to about 18 out of every 100 who took the placebo. However, NSAIDs also caused more side effects like upset stomach and headaches. About 11 to 14 out of every 100 women who took NSAIDs had side effects, compared to about 10 out of every 100 who took the placebo. 

When different types of NSAIDs were compared, there wasn't enough strong evidence to show one type was clearly better than the others. Also, there weren't enough studies comparing COX-2 specific NSAIDs to regular NSAIDs or paracetamol to see which might be safer or more effective. Most of the studies were paid for by companies, which could affect how they reported their results.

Overall, NSAIDs seem to be a good option for relieving menstrual pain, but women need to be aware that they can cause side effects. More research is needed to figure out which type of NSAID might be safest and most effective. The evidence isn't very strong because many studies didn't report their methods clearly.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with 9,839 people who had moderate to severe COPD. Most studies didn't have people who had just had a flare-up of their condition. Many of the studies were paid for by drug companies, which means they might not be completely fair. The main studies included people who weren't having a flare-up. The results show that using a medicine called LAMA plus another type of medicine (LAMA+LABA) instead of just the other medicine (LABA+ICS) helped reduce flare-ups by about 18%. It also helped people breathe better and lowered the chance of getting pneumonia. People also reported feeling better overall. However, the evidence isn't perfect because some studies had problems like not being fair or not telling us everything. So, while it seems helpful, we need more studies to be sure. This information supports new guidelines for treating COPD.

output: This review looked at how well a medicine called PEP helps prevent HIV infection after a possible exposure. It found that getting a lot of damage to your skin during the procedure, seeing blood on the equipment, doing procedures that put a needle in the source person's blood, and if the source person has a serious illness can increase the chance of HIV spreading. However, even after adjusting for these risks, the medicine didn't seem to help stop HIV from spreading better than a placebo. Also, people who got the medicine were less likely to take it. The review suggests that healthcare workers should start taking PEP right away after a possible exposure, especially if there's a high chance of HIV spreading. But there isn't strong proof that taking more than one type of medicine works better. Healthcare workers should be told about the side effects they might have and how to deal with them. They shouldn't expect PEP to work perfectly. Since it's hard to do a big study to prove it works, healthcare workers should talk to their doctors about the best way to handle a possible HIV exposure. More research is needed to learn more about the side effects and to look at animal studies too.

output: This review looked at 11 studies with 855 participants. output: This review looked at how parents feel about getting vaccines for their children. Most parents want more information about vaccines than they get, and lack of information can make them worried or regretful about vaccinating their kids. They prefer balanced information that explains both the good and bad parts of vaccines, presented simply and tailored to their situation. Parents want vaccination information in more places, like outside of regular health services, and they want it before each visit. Health workers are important sources of information, but parents expect them to communicate well. Sometimes, poor communication or bad relationships with health workers can affect vaccination decisions. Parents often struggle to trust different sources of information and find it hard to get unbiased advice. Generally, parents who are less sure about vaccines want more information. The review found that most programs tried to improve one or two ways of communicating about vaccines, like giving information before appointments and tailoring it to parents. But they didn't address negative news stories or how parents think about why health workers do things. To help more parents feel comfortable with vaccines, planners should think about when to give information, where to find it, how to present it clearly and fairly, and how parents see health workers. More research is needed, especially in areas with fewer resources.

Some studies found that screening didn't reduce breast cancer deaths, while others suggested it might lower them a little bit. But the studies with better ways of picking who gets screened sometimes didn't find any benefit. 

Screening led to more surgeries, like removing part of the breast (lumpectomy) or the whole breast (mastectomy), but not more chemotherapy. About 200 extra women might get treated unnecessarily, and more than 200 might feel worried about their health. 

The leaflet we made explains the pros and cons of screening so people can make a decision. Since new treatments have come out and more people know about breast cancer, the benefits of screening might be smaller now. Studies done recently show more women might be overdiagnosed and less advanced cancer might be found. So, while screening might still be helpful, it's not as clear-cut as it once was.

output: This review looked at four studies that compared using a steroid medicine on the eye with not using it for bacterial eye infections called keratitis. The studies involved a total of about 612 people. None of the studies found that using the steroid medicine made a big difference in how well people could see or in how much the infection healed. One study found that people who didn't use the steroid medicine healed faster. But another large study didn't find this difference. None of the studies found that using the steroid medicine caused more problems. Some studies lost track of some people, which might have affected the results. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say whether using the steroid medicine helps or hurts in treating bacterial eye infections. More studies with better designs are needed to get clearer answers.

output: Three small studies looked at using intramedullary nailing versus plating for fractures in the lower leg. The studies had some problems that made it hard to trust their results. The studies didn't find clear differences in how well patients did, like walking or feeling pain. Nailing seemed to lead to fewer surgeries for problems later, but the studies weren't big enough to be sure. The studies also didn't show a clear difference in how often the bones healed properly. Because the studies had limitations and were small, we're not sure if one method is better than the other. More studies are needed to help decide which method might work best for these types of fractures in adults.

This review looked at 15 studies with 1835 cancer patients to see if certain treatments helped people return to work (RTW) or improve their quality of life. Most of the studies were about breast or prostate cancer. Some studies taught patients about their condition and helped them take care of themselves, while others gave patients exercise programs or made changes to their treatment plans. The studies found that:

- Teaching patients about their condition and helping them take care of themselves didn't seem to help them return to work better than usual care.
- A physical training program for breast cancer patients didn't help them return to work more than usual care.
- Less aggressive treatment for breast or prostate cancer patients didn't make it easier for them to return to work compared to more aggressive treatment.
- Combining different types of help like counseling, education, and exercise didn't seem to help patients return to work more than usual care.
- This type of combined help did seem to help patients return to work more often than usual care.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say these treatments definitely help patients return to work or improve their quality of life. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at how doctors ask patients about side effects after taking medicine. It found that asking patients more specifically about their symptoms led to more side effects being reported. Some side effects were reported only when patients were asked more thoroughly. However, it's not clear if this affects whether the side effects are big enough to matter. The review suggests that how doctors ask questions can affect what side effects are reported. Using more detailed questions might lead to fewer important side effects being missed. But it's not clear if this changes what kind of side effects are reported. The review had some limitations because the studies used different ways to ask questions. To get clearer results, future studies should use clear definitions for side effects and report how they were measured. They should also make sure the way they ask questions is easy for both doctors and patients to do.

output: This review looked at 15 studies with 721 people who had pain from different kinds of cancer. Most studies were done on adults, not children. While the studies were generally well-done, many had small numbers of people and some had problems keeping track of missing information or people leaving the studies. Most studies gave codeine, sometimes with paracetamol, and compared it to a sugar pill or other medicines. Some studies lasted for just one day, while others lasted longer. Codeine seemed to help reduce pain better than a sugar pill, but was about the same as other medicines. But the studies didn't always report if people got sick from the medicine. Nausea, vomiting, and constipation were common side effects, especially in longer studies. Only a few studies had enough good information to look at carefully. Overall, codeine seems to work better than nothing for cancer pain, but it can cause these uncomfortable side effects. More studies are needed to know how well it works over time and if it's safe for everyone. There's not much information for children.

output: This review looked at studies that tried to make food and drinks easier to swallow for people with dementia. But no new studies were found that specifically looked at making food or drinks thicker. Instead, two studies looked at how different thicknesses of liquids affected swallowing problems. One study found that thicker liquids helped prevent choking during meals, but another study found that people who drank very thick liquids had more chest infections. Both studies had some flaws, so we can't be sure if thickening liquids helps or hurts. The studies didn't look at how it affects the person's quality of life. It seems that making liquids thicker might help people swallow better right away, but we don't know if this helps in the long run. More studies are needed to find out if thickening liquids is safe and helpful for people with dementia.

This review looked at 50 studies involving 12,877 people with high cholesterol levels. The studies tested how well a medicine called cerivastatin worked to lower bad cholesterol (LDL), good cholesterol (HDL), and fats called triglycerides. Most of the studies found that taking cerivastatin helped lower these levels. The evidence for these findings is considered very strong. 

Cerivastatin worked better than other similar medicines like fluvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin. It was especially effective at lowering LDL cholesterol. Cerivastatin also increased good cholesterol (HDL) by about 5%.

However, the studies had some problems. Many didn't tell us if people stopped taking the medicine because of side effects. But even then, the number of people who stopped taking cerivastatin because of side effects was not much higher than those who stopped taking a placebo.

The effect of cerivastatin on lowering cholesterol was closely related to how much of the medicine people took. The medicine was most effective when taken in larger doses.

Overall, cerivastatin seemed to be very good at lowering cholesterol, but we don't know much about its safety because the studies were short and didn't always report side effects. More research is needed to fully understand both the benefits and risks of cerivastatin.

output: This review looked at 10 trials with 599 people who have anorexia nervosa. Some of the trials were new, and others were updated. Two of the trials involved children. The trials tested different types of talk therapy, but it's hard to compare them because they weren't always done the same way. Most of the trials had problems where the people giving the therapy didn't know if the person was getting the real therapy or not, and some people dropped out of the trials. The review suggests that a type of therapy called psychodynamic therapy might help more than usual care given by doctors who don't specialize in eating disorders. But other types of therapy, like cognitive analytic therapy, didn't seem to work better. Some types of therapy, like Optimized Treatment as Usual (Optimized TAU) given by experts, worked as well as cognitive behavior therapy. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say which type of therapy works best. More and larger trials are needed to find out.

Overall, the evidence suggests that magnesium doesn't provide a clear benefit for preventing muscle cramps in most people.

- Some studies compared self-managed OHA to professional OHA. Again, there wasn't much good evidence to show one was better.
- Finally, some studies compared more intensive one-on-one OHA to regular one-on-one OHA. There wasn't enough good evidence to show one was better.

RhGH seemed to help with some breathing problems and made kids grow taller, but didn't make them heavier or have better lung function. It helped with their weight and body muscle, but only when compared to not taking anything. RhGH might also lower blood sugar levels, but not enough to cause diabetes. 

There was some evidence that rhGH helped prevent breathing problems, but the trials were too short to know if this would last. It didn't seem to improve how kids felt or how well they could exercise. 

One trial suggested rhGH might improve how kids felt, but the results weren't clear. Overall, rhGH seems to help with growing taller and making kids stronger, but not much else. More long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and see if the benefits outweigh the risks.

This review looked at three trials that tested a special balloon with medicine (paclitaxel) to treat a problem called in-stent restenosis in leg arteries. The trials were done in Germany and Austria, and two companies made the special balloons. The trials looked at whether the special balloon helped more than regular balloons. 

The results showed that the special balloon didn't help prevent amputations or deaths. But it seemed to help keep the artery open longer (target lesion revascularization) and reduce blockages (binary restenosis) for up to 24 months. It also helped improve how well people could walk (improvement in Rutherford category) for up to 12 months. 

However, the evidence isn't very strong because there weren't many people in the trials, and the way the trials were done might have been a bit biased. More and bigger trials are needed to know if the special balloon really works better.

Overall, there isn't much good evidence about what works best to prevent and treat IAD. Soap and water didn't seem to work well. To get better answers, we need more high-quality studies that use similar methods and test the same things. We also need to agree on what information to look for in these studies to make comparisons easier. The information in this review is up to date as of September 28, 2016.

This review looked at different tests that can help find malaria, especially a type called P. falciparum. The tests are made using different parts of the malaria parasite. We found 74 studies that tested these tests against a method called microscopy, which is considered the gold standard. 

For tests that look for HRP-2 (a part of the parasite), the studies showed that these tests are very good at finding malaria. They correctly identify about 95 out of every 100 infected people (high sensitivity) and correctly rule out malaria in about 95 out of every 100 healthy people (high specificity). 

For tests that look for pLDH (another part of the parasite), they are even better. They correctly identify about 98 out of every 100 infected people and correctly rule out malaria in about 98 out of every 100 healthy people. 

However, these tests can sometimes give false positives, meaning they might say someone has malaria when they don't. For HRP-2 tests, this happens in about 3 out of every 100 people who don't have malaria. For pLDH tests, it happens in about 1 out of every 100 people who don't have malaria. 

Overall, these tests are very good at finding malaria, but they might sometimes give wrong answers. They can be used to help doctors diagnose malaria, but they might not be perfect. More studies are needed to confirm these results and to find the best way to use these tests.

output: This review looked at 15 studies with 3057 people to see if taking antibiotics helps treat a stuffy nose and sinus problems (rhinosinusitis). Most studies were done well. Without antibiotics, about half of people got better after a week and 64% after two weeks. Antibiotics helped people get better faster, but only about 5 to 11 out of every 100 people who took them got better faster compared to those who didn't take them. Antibiotics worked better when doctors could see pus in the sinuses using a special test. But, more people had side effects like upset stomach when taking antibiotics. About 13 more people had side effects than those who didn't take antibiotics. Antibiotics also lowered the chance of getting worse, but it wasn't clear if this was helpful. There was one case where someone got a brain infection after taking antibiotics. While antibiotics might help a bit, the benefits aren't strong enough to use them for most people with a stuffy nose and sinus problems. The review couldn't make a clear decision about children, people with weak immune systems, or those with very bad sinus problems because those groups weren't studied.

This review looked at 70 studies with 44,958 participants and 63 studies with 42,784 participants. Most of these studies had moderate or low quality evidence. The review focused on outcomes four or more months after the intervention to see if the effects lasted. It found that social norm interventions might help reduce some alcohol-related problems. Specifically:

- They helped decrease alcohol problems by about 1.28 points on a scale (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.04).
- They reduced binge drinking by about 2.7% (SMD -0.06, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.02).
- They led to a slight reduction in the number of drinks consumed each week (SMD -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.04).
- They decreased the number of drinking days per week (WF: SMD -0.11, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.04; IFF: SMD -0.21, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.10).

However, the effects were small and not always consistent. The review suggests that while there might be some benefits, they are not large enough to make a big difference in preventing alcohol misuse among college students. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

Most studies found that short-term use of corticosteroids (for 3 to 7 days) did not lead to more treatment failures or relapses compared to longer-term use (10 to 15 days). One study found that short-term use might lead to about 22 fewer treatment failures for every 1000 people. Another study found no difference in the number of times people had another COPD flare-up after treatment. Some studies also found that short-term use did not lead to more side effects. Short-term use did not seem to affect how long people stayed in the hospital or their lung function. Based on these findings, it seems that five days of oral corticosteroids might be enough for treating adults with acute COPD flare-ups. However, more research is needed to confirm this and to compare it with longer courses of corticosteroids. The evidence is considered moderate because it's not very precise, and more studies are needed to be sure.

output: This review looked at 12 studies involving 3259 patients with type 2 diabetes. The studies compared regular blood sugar checks (SMBG) with usual care that didn't include checking blood sugar. Some studies checked blood sugar daily, others weekly. Most studies were done fairly well. For patients with diabetes for at least a year, regular blood sugar checks seemed to lower their blood sugar levels a little bit, but not much. After 12 months, this effect went away. Checking blood sugar didn't seem to improve how patients felt or their overall health. Two studies looked at costs and found that checking blood sugar daily cost more money than checking it less often. Overall, regular blood sugar checks might help a little bit in the short term, but not much longer. Checking blood sugar doesn't seem to make patients feel better or have better overall health. More research is needed to understand the effects of regular blood sugar checks on mental health and other important aspects of living with diabetes.

output: This review looked at ten studies involving 3340 people. Some studies compared aripiprazole alone to a placebo, while others compared it to other medicines like lithium or haloperidol. Most studies lost some participants, which might affect the results. Aripiprazole helped reduce symptoms of mania in both adults and children/teens after three and four weeks, but not after six weeks. When compared to other medicines, aripiprazole didn't show better results in reducing mania symptoms. Aripiprazole caused more movement problems, like shaky hands, compared to a placebo. It also caused more stomach issues like nausea and constipation, and sometimes lowered a child's or teen's milk-making hormone levels. The studies had some differences that made it hard to compare all the results. By 12 weeks, aripiprazole didn't cause more movement problems than lithium, but it still caused more movement problems than haloperidol. Overall, aripiprazole seems to help with mania symptoms, but it has some side effects that people need to consider. More studies comparing it to other medicines are needed to know where it fits best in treatment.

This review looked at five studies comparing crowns to fillings in people with tooth problems. Four studies used permanent metal crowns (PMCs), and two used crowns made with a special technique called the Hall Technique. The studies found that crowns were better than fillings in the long run. - Crowns were less likely to fail or cause pain compared to fillings.
- Crowns caused less discomfort during the procedure, especially when made using the Hall Technique.
- There was some uncertainty about whether crowns caused more bleeding around the gums compared to fillings, but the evidence wasn’t strong enough to say for sure.

Crowns were also compared to not doing anything to treat the tooth problem. This comparison didn’t have enough good-quality evidence to draw clear conclusions.

Overall, crowns seem to be a better choice than fillings for long-term protection of teeth, reducing the risk of problems like failing or causing pain. Using the Hall Technique might make the procedure less painful. But there isn’t enough good-quality evidence to say if crowns are better than not treating the tooth, or if metal crowns are better than ones with a shiny outer layer. More studies are needed to get clearer answers.

So while hyaluronan seems helpful, more research is needed to know exactly how it works and if it's safe for everyone. Overall, hyaluronan appears to be a good option for treating knee OA, but it's important to talk to a doctor about the best choice for each person.

output: This review looked at 19 studies involving 3480 people with brain injuries. Most of the studies were well-designed, but some were not. For people with milder brain injuries, getting good information helps them recover well without needing extra special treatments. For those with more severe injuries, getting formal help works better, and starting rehab early usually leads to better results. People in rehab for moderate to severe injuries who get more intense treatment tend to improve faster. A special type of rehab called milieu-oriented, where patients do rehab in a supportive environment with peers, seems to work well for those with severe injuries. But it's hard to test these ideas in all cases because some people might need special care that isn't easily replaced. Different people have different problems after a brain injury, so they need different kinds of help. People with mild injuries should follow up and get advice. Those with moderate to severe injuries should have regular check-ups to plan their rehab. More intense rehab early on seems to help, but we don't know if it's worth the extra cost. Patients who finish inpatient rehab should have access to outpatient or community-based services. Group-based rehab in a supportive environment helps people with severe brain injuries. Some questions about rehab can't be answered by experiments, like which treatments work best for everyone over time. Future research will need to look at real-world data from ongoing care to answer these questions.

The studies explored how people liked digital health programs, like getting reminders for medicine or appointments. Some people said these programs made them feel supported and helped them connect with others. But many people had problems using these programs. They couldn't always get cell networks or internet, or didn't have phones. Sometimes their phones were taken away by others. The cost of messages was also a big issue, and many people wanted them to be free. Language and phone skills were another problem. People were worried about privacy when it came to health topics like HIV or family planning. To solve these problems, some people suggested using simple language, sending messages at good times, and choosing the right way to deliver the messages. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that digital health programs can help with feelings of support and connection, but there are many challenges to making them work well. Program planners need to think about these challenges when creating programs. Future studies should try to fix these problems and tell us how they did so.

output: This review looked at 83 studies, but only 5 were included because they compared laser treatment to no treatment. These studies involved 4786 people with diabetes who had retinopathy. Laser treatment helped reduce the risk of losing vision by about half after 12 months (though this wasn't true for everyone). It also helped prevent severe vision loss and slowed down the progression of retinopathy. However, the studies weren't perfect because they didn't have a fair comparison group. The benefits were mostly seen in people with a more advanced form of retinopathy. The evidence isn't very strong because the studies are old and newer treatments might be better. More research is needed to see if combining laser treatment with newer treatments like anti-VEGFs could work even better.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 349 participants with urinary catheters. Most studies had some problems in how they were done, making it hard to trust the results fully. The studies mostly looked at whether using different liquids to clean out the catheter (washouts) helps prevent infections or makes the catheter last longer. Some studies compared different types of washouts, like using salt water or acidic solutions, but the results weren't clear. The studies didn't look at things like how many times the catheter was used or how well patients liked using the washouts. Because the studies had some flaws, we can't be sure if washouts help or hurt. We need more well-designed studies to find out if washouts are helpful or harmful.

output: This review looked at 13 small studies and 3 ongoing ones that tested tai chi for heart health. Most studies had problems being sure if they were fair, and some didn't report everything clearly. The studies mostly involved healthy people, but some included those with high blood pressure, older adults at risk of falls, or those with certain types of heart trouble. Few studies looked at serious heart problems like death or major health issues. Blood pressure and cholesterol levels were measured in many studies, but the results weren't always clear. Some studies found that tai chi helped lower blood pressure and cholesterol, while others found no difference or even a small increase. One study found that tai chi improved quality of life after three months. But none of the studies looked at whether tai chi affects the risk of heart disease or diabetes. Because the studies were small and had some flaws, we don't have enough strong evidence to say tai chi helps prevent heart disease. More and better studies are needed to learn more about tai chi's effects on heart health.

This review looked at 66 studies from 1988 to 2012 that studied how well endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) works in finding different stages of stomach cancer. EUS is a tool doctors use to see inside the stomach. The studies were mostly done well, but some had small problems. 

For EUS to tell if cancer has spread deep into the stomach wall (T3-T4), it was very good at doing so. It correctly identified these cancers 86 out of 100 times. For cancers that have grown into the muscle layer (T1-T2), it was even better, correct 90 out of 100 times. 

When trying to find cancers that have just reached the surface (T1a) or are growing deeper (T1b), EUS was still quite good, correct 87 out of 100 times. But for cancers that have spread to nearby lymph nodes (N-stage), it wasn't as good, correct 83 out of 100 times.

Overall, EUS helps doctors know more about where stomach cancer is located, which is helpful. But the results vary a lot between studies, so we can't be sure it's always accurate. Also, it's not as good at telling if a cancer is just on the surface or has grown deeper, or if lymph nodes have cancer. More research is needed to understand why the results differ so much.

output: A study with 46 people who have sickle cell disease found that those taking vitamin D3 had higher levels of a vitamin D chemical in their blood compared to those taking a sugar pill. Vitamin D3 helped increase vitamin D levels by about 29.79 units after eight weeks, 12.67 units after sixteen weeks, and 15.52 units after twenty-four weeks. This suggests vitamin D might help improve vitamin D levels in people with sickle cell disease. However, the study had some problems, like not having enough people finish the full six months of the study. There were no major side effects reported, but the evidence for this is not very strong. The study also looked at how much pain people had, and those taking vitamin D had less pain days, but again, the evidence is not very strong. The study didn't look at how well people felt overall, but those taking vitamin D had worse health-related quality of life scores, especially after sixteen and twenty-four weeks. Because this is just one study with some issues, it's not enough to make doctors give vitamin D to everyone with sickle cell disease. Doctors should use existing guidelines and advice about vitamin D supplements. More high-quality studies are needed to know if vitamin D helps and is safe for people with sickle cell disease.

This review looked at three studies that treated children with a condition called neuroblastoma. The studies compared two types of treatment: myeloablative therapy (a strong treatment that destroys bone marrow) and conventional chemotherapy. The studies found that myeloablative therapy might help children live longer without their cancer coming back (event-free survival), but it didn't seem to give them a better chance of surviving for a longer time (overall survival) after the initial treatment. 

When researchers looked at more information from one of the studies, they still saw that myeloablative therapy helped prevent the cancer from coming back. But they couldn't find enough information to say if it helped children live longer overall.

The studies didn't find any clear differences in serious side effects like infections or kidney problems. However, they did see more of these side effects in the group that got myeloablative therapy.

The studies also didn't look at how well the children felt or how their lives were affected by the treatments. Some of the studies had problems that might make the results less reliable.

Based on what we know now, myeloablative therapy might help prevent the cancer from coming back, but it's not clear if it helps children live longer. More research is needed to figure out the best way to treat this condition, especially since the definition of "high-risk" has changed. Future studies should be done carefully to make sure they're comparing apples to apples and follow patients for a long time to get a clearer picture.

output: This review looked at nine studies involving 1512 women who were trying to get pregnant. Most studies involved women who were having fertility treatments like IUI (intrauterine insemination). The studies mostly compared a procedure called intentional endometrial injury, where the lining of the uterus is slightly damaged, to no damage or a fake procedure. The results are not very clear if this procedure helps women get pregnant or have a baby. Some studies suggested it might help, but the evidence isn't strong enough to be sure. The studies showed that the procedure might make it easier for some women to get pregnant, but the evidence for this is also not very good. The pain during the procedure was usually not very bad, around a 6 out of 10. But only one study reported this. The timing of the procedure didn't seem to matter much. The studies didn't find any evidence that this procedure increases the risk of miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or twins. Overall, we're not sure if this procedure helps women get pregnant or have a baby. More studies are needed to know for sure.

output: This review looked at 42 studies with 4220 participants to see how well a type of ultrasound called CDUS and another called CE-CDUS work in detecting a condition called endoleak. Most of the studies were not very good because it was hard to know if the doctors were blind to the results or if they knew which test was done first. The studies that used CDUS found that the test was about 82% accurate for picking up endoleaks and 93% accurate for ruling them out. The studies that used CE-CDUS found it was 94% accurate for picking up endoleaks and 95% accurate for ruling them out. Using contrast made the CDUS test much better at finding endoleaks. The studies that used CE-CDUS were better done than those that used CDUS. The studies that used CDUS got better results before 2006 compared to those that used it after 2006. When looking at the studies that used scans instead of individual participants, the results were similar. Overall, CE-CDUS seems to be better at finding endoleaks than CDUS. So, for checking endoleaks, using CE-CDUS might be a good choice first, followed by a CT scan if the ultrasound is positive.

output: This review looked at 25 studies involving 3663 children. Most studies were done well and fairly. The results show that children who took oral antibiotics were more likely to have their ear infections go away completely after two to three months compared to those who didn't take antibiotics (2 out of every 5 children benefited). But, they were also more likely to get side effects like diarrhea, vomiting, or a rash (about 20 children would need to take antibiotics for one child to get these side effects). Antibiotics seemed to help children's ears heal faster, but it wasn't clear if they helped hearing. Antibiotics didn't seem to cause more problems like needing tubes in the ears or having more ear infections later. However, the benefits of antibiotics for ear infections might not last as long as we thought. It's important to weigh the good and bad effects of antibiotics and consider whether they're really necessary for treating ear infections.

This review looked at 40 new studies and 7 ongoing ones. It included 63 studies in total, focusing on regional anesthesia to prevent pain problems (PPP) after surgeries. The studies showed that:

- For surgeries like thoracotomies, using epidural anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 18 months (odds ratio [OR] 0.52, meaning it's about half as likely to happen).
- For breast cancer surgeries, regional anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 12 months (OR 0.43).
- For cesarean sections, regional anesthesia might help reduce PPP for up to 8 months (OR 0.46).

However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if other types of surgeries or different anesthesia methods work. The studies had some flaws, so we're not completely sure about the results. More and better studies are needed to make stronger conclusions.

This review looked at six studies with a total of 137 people to see if a treatment called tDCS helps with Parkinson's disease. The studies mostly compared tDCS to a fake treatment (called sham tDCS). Here’s what they found:

- tDCS didn't seem to help with overall symptoms of Parkinson's (like how well someone can move).
- tDCS did seem to help with specific parts of movement, like how fast someone can walk.
- tDCS didn't help with how much time someone spends without symptoms (off time) or with involuntary movements (on time).
- tDCS didn't improve how well people do everyday tasks.
- tDCS didn't seem to make health-related quality of life better.
- tDCS didn't cause more people to stop taking part in the study or have bad side effects compared to the fake treatment.

Overall, the evidence isn’t strong enough to say tDCS works well for Parkinson's disease. More studies are needed to learn more about it.

output: This review looked at 18 studies involving 4843 participants to see if taking bisphosphonates helped reduce pain or other problems in people with bone issues. While bisphosphonates didn't seem to make much difference in how many people got better from pain, they did seem to help prevent something called skeletal-related events, which are bad things that happen to bones. Bisphosphonates also didn't seem to affect how long people lived. However, they caused more nausea and kidney problems. The studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure if these effects are really big or just small. Bisphosphonates might help keep the bones from getting worse, but we need more studies to confirm this. It's important to weigh the potential benefits against the side effects like nausea and kidney trouble. Future studies should use the same ways to measure how people feel to get clearer answers.

This review looked at 112 studies about heart failure treatments for people with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Most studies didn't do a good job of comparing treatments fairly. The studies mostly looked at heart failure in adults, but some included people with CKD. Here's what we know:

- For heart failure in general, some medicines like adenosine A1-receptor antagonists, dopamine, nesiritide, and serelaxin don't seem to help much or have mixed effects.
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) might not help or might even make things worse in some cases.
- Beta-blockers might help lower the risk of dying from heart problems.
- Aldosterone antagonists might raise the chance of having too much potassium in the blood.
- Vasopressin receptor antagonists might not affect heart failure or kidney health.
- Sinus node inhibitors haven't been studied enough to know if they affect potassium levels.
- Other treatments like digoxin, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, renin inhibitors, and vasodilators haven't been studied well enough to know their effects.

Overall, we're not sure if these treatments work well for people with both heart failure and CKD. More studies are needed to better understand how different treatments might affect people with CKD who have heart failure.

output: This review looked at five trials that included a total of 3427 adults with a type of cancer called Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). The trials compared two different chemotherapy treatments: one called BEACOPP escalated and another called ABVD. The BEACOPP escalated treatment seemed to help people live longer and feel better for a longer time. It also helped stop the cancer from spreading faster. However, the BEACOPP escalated treatment caused more serious side effects like low blood counts and infections. The review found that about 90 out of every 100 people who got the BEACOPP escalated treatment would still be alive after five years, compared to about 120 out of every 100 people who got the ABVD treatment. But the review couldn't tell if the BEACOPP escalated treatment caused more infertility or if it was better for men's fertility. The review also couldn't say for sure if the BEACOPP escalated treatment caused more secondary cancers, but it suggested it might. Overall, the review found that the BEACOPP escalated treatment might be better for people with advanced HL, but more research is needed to know for sure.

This review looked at 10 studies that tested different antibiotics to help prevent lung infections in children who are at high risk. The studies involved children with HIV, cystic fibrosis, cancer, sickle cell disease, and low birth weight babies with breathing problems. The studies lasted from 7 days to 3 years. Some studies had better methods than others. 

For children with HIV, there wasn't much difference in getting lung infections if they took certain antibiotics. But taking co-trimoxazole or isoniazid didn't seem to affect their chances of dying. Antibiotics like co-trimoxazole might actually lower the chance of dying. 

Children with cystic fibrosis who took ciprofloxacin had fewer lung infections. Azithromycin helped reduce flare-ups of their lungs. But it didn't always help with growth. There was a small chance that the bacteria might become stronger after taking the antibiotics. 

For children with sickle cell disease, taking penicillin V seemed to lower the chance of getting a type of blood infection called pneumococcal septicaemia. 

For children with cancer, taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole helped lower the chance of a lung infection called Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that certain antibiotics can help reduce lung infections, flare-ups, and hospital stays in some high-risk children. But the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure that antibiotics work in all cases. More studies are needed to find out if antibiotics help prevent lung infections in other high-risk groups like those with heart defects, metabolic disorders, or prematurity.

output: This review looked at studies about how often certain bad things happen to kidneys after some treatments for cancer. It found that the chances of kidney problems can vary a lot depending on the type of cancer, the treatment, and how long people are followed. Some studies found that kidney function might get worse, while others didn't. Common problems include changes in how well the kidneys work, too much protein in the urine, and not enough calcium or magnesium in the blood. Some treatments like radiation to the kidney area, taking away part of the kidney, and certain medicines called platinum drugs seem to increase the risk of these problems. But the studies weren't always done the same way, so it's hard to know for sure which treatments cause the most problems. More research is needed to better understand which treatments might harm the kidneys and how to prevent it. Patients should be followed closely after treatment to check their kidney health and blood pressure.
